Ten glorious minutes when Seika looks like the school in the pamphlets — clean lines, bright halls, the flagpole catching light like it's posing. Then the ten minutes end, and the real Seika comes back: the radiator in the second-floor hallway that only works when it feels like it, the vending machine on the first floor that eats exactly one coin a week like some kind of offering, the announcement speaker that crackles before every morning greeting, as if clearing its throat.

The main building has three wings. The north wing is where you'll find everything anyone cares about — the culture club rooms, the art room with its ever-smelling turpentine, and the music room whose upright piano has a fourth-floor view and a third-floor attitude. The south wing is academics, mostly: math, Japanese, the chemistry lab where we once evacuated because someone — I will never say who — left a beaker unattended. The east wing is the one nobody mentions in tours, because it's mostly storage and the teachers' lounge, and because the stairwell there is where the older students go to cry before exams. I know because I've used it.

My classroom is 3-B, second floor, north side, which means in spring the cherry tree outside my window drops petals onto my desk if I leave it open, and in summer it blocks the worst of the afternoon heat. The class has thirty-two students, and I could tell you where every one of them sits and why: Hana by the door because she's always five minutes late, Riku in the back corner because he naps, and me — third row, window seat, because everyone knows the window seat belongs to whoever notices things first.

It taught me that the school has a rhythm: the way the hallway noise swells at 8:15 and drops the moment the first teacher's footsteps echo; the way the gymsarium lights buzz off at 6 p.m. sharp whether club practice is done or not; the way everyone pretends not to look at the bulletin board when the culture festival pairings go up.

People say Seika is an ordinary school. Local, mid-sized, nothing special — no famous alumni, no national tournament banners, no histories in textbooks. But I've decided that's exactly what I love about it. Ordinary schools are where everything actually happens first. Friendships. Rivalries. The small brave things that will matter to you forever and to no one else.

So that's my school. Seika High — groaning gate, stubborn radiators, one thieving vending machine, and a cherry tree that keeps its appointments better than most people do.

**Chapter 4: The Day of Open Doors**

By the time the first guests came through the old iron gate, I had already taped my thumb to a cardboard sign twice.

"Welcome to Seika High," I said, for the eleventh time. The sign said WELCOME TO SEIKA HIGH. My thumb said nothing, but it throbbed in a way that suggested it disagreed with the lettering.

"You're holding it crooked," Ren said, sliding the door open with one hand and balancing a stack of haunted house flyers on the other. Class 3-B had, in a parliamentary disaster I still didn't fully understand, voted to run a combined café-and-haunted-house. Nobody could explain how both halves fit in one classroom. Nobody had to. The cherry tree outside our window had been designated the waiting area, which mostly meant it was now full of first-years eating yakisoba and judging us.

"I'm holding it straight," I said. "The doorframe is crooked. This whole building is crooked."

"That's charm. Write that down for the pamphlet."

A woman with two small children passed through, and the smaller one stopped, pointed at the sign, and said, "That girl is bleeding tape."

"Adhesive," I told her gravely. "It's adhesive."

She looked at me the way you look at a vending machine that has just eaten your coin — which, incidentally, happened to me at 10:40, because I was thirsty and the machine by the east stairwell is the only one on our side and it has taken one hundred and ten yen from me across the school year like a slow, patient debt collector. Ren shook it. The machine shook back. A can of corn soup dropped out, which neither of us wanted and both of us now owned.

That was the morning. The afternoon was where it stopped being a project and started being a day.

The class had debated for two weeks whether the haunted house should be scary or funny, and we'd settled on neither: it was populated entirely by second-years wearing newspaper costumes and delivering lines off cribs held in shaking hands. It should have been a humiliation. Instead, when a girl in a newspaper kimono misdelivered her line — "BEHOLD, the curse of the chemistry lab" — and a senior guest laughed so hard he had to sit down on our prop broom and break it, something warm moved through the room. The fcrowd followed the laugh. Crowds always do.

I was on café duty after the four o'clock rotation, which meant I spent an hour saying "the blended lemon is just lemon, ice, and faith" to strangers who invariably ordered it. A boy from the north culture clubs — orchestra, I thought, from the rosin smell that trailed him — ordered it and then stood there drinking it very slowly and clearly not liking it and ordering a second one anyway.

"You don't have to do that," I said.

"It's good," he said.

"It's lemon and faith."

"That's what I like about it." He looked at the tree outside the window. "You get to see this every day?"

"Every day it isn't taped to something."

He laughed, paid for the second cup, and left a five-yen coin on the counter like a tip, which is not a thing you can do in Japan, and which our class treasurer later spent ten minutes trying to refuse.

At five, when the corridors were at their loudest and the light through the east windows had gone the color of weak tea, I took the stairs I always take. Not because I was upset. Because some habits have better views. From the east-wing stairwell landing you could hear the whole school at once — the gym band butting up against the brass club butting up against someone's posso-ka rehearsal of a song none of them fully knew — and for once, nobody was in this stairwell crying before exams. It was just me and the noise and the strange peace of a building that had decided, for one day, to let people in.

Ren found me there at five-twenty, holding two cups of blended lemon.

"You're missing the punchline of the year," she said. "Sato-san's balloon art collapsed. In front of the principal. It looked like—" she paused, "—actually it looked like the chemistry curse. Full circle."

"Give me a minute."

"We don't have a minute, the second-years are panicking and someone put the corn soup in the haunted house."

I looked at the two cups. I took both, because it seemed rude to make her carry her own.

"Which is the faith one?" I asked.

"They're both just lemon, Mia."

I decided not to tell her. Some things you keep for the next chapter.

I wasn't scheduled for anything this morning. That's the accident of the day: Mizuki's class is running the café, they asked for extra hands, and she cornered me at the shoe lockers before I could invent an errand. So now I'm carrying trays through a room remade into something almost unrecognizable — tablecloths, a hand-drawn menu, the coin-eating vending machine in the corner wearing a fruit crown someone made for it.

"That machine," I tell Mizuki, nodding at it. "It ate three hundred yen of mine this spring."

"It's paying its debt," she says. "Order of cocoa, ma'am."

The room fills by ten. What surprises me is the talking — classmates I've shared a classroom with for two years without learning their first names are suddenly arguing about whether the pancakes are "autumn-flavored" or "flavored autumn." I pour tea and listen. Understated works fine for a job like this.

At two, Mizuki orders me on break, "Grumpy waiter face is bad for business," so I walk the halls. The north wing smells like paint and cardboard. The graduation-years exhibit is mostly photos andorque — and then I stop, because there's a photo of 3-B's cherry tree I've never seen: spring, petals, someone's joke of a shadow caught mid-leap beneath it. No name on the card. Someone was there when I wasn't looking, or I was there when I never noticed.

The haunted house, naturally, is a desk-and-cardboard maze in the third-year science prep room, and I find Ren standing outside holding the door like a butler at a slightly deranged party.

"You volunteered to help them," I say.

"And you visited," he says. "Who's dumber?"

"Still you. I got roped into it."

He looks past me, into the dark. "Kayo built the jump-scare. The one at the end. She kept it secret even from us."

Kayo — the quiet one from the astronomy club who sits two seats ahead of me and has said maybe forty words to me in two years. The girl who built the thing in the dark that's making fourth-years scream. I stand there holding my half-empty tray, feeling something shift in how big the school is. Larger inside, today, than the floor plan says.

"Go on," Ren says, grinning. "Group of first-years going in. Watch the door."

I watch the door. The screams are real, and the laughter after them is realer. Outside a window, three floors down, the gymsarium lights are on for the first time past six in weeks — nobody wants the day to end.

Tomorrow the cardboard comes down and the school goes back to being gray and ordinary. But that's fine, I think. I finally learned the trick to festivals — you have to be carrying something, a tray or a hammer, to be in them instead of just walking past.
